KXNCAAFSECWINS, BIGTENWINS, BIG12WINS and ACCWINS (sampled rungs 8+, 7+, 5+ teams with 10+ wins, regular season only per the rules text) need a joint schedule simulation, not a single-game margin model.

KXNCAAFD3GAME and KXNCAAFCSGAME are winner markets on teams outside FBS data coverage; their probability comes from this score-based rating, not from SP+ or PPA.

interactions.hypothesis: QB status x spread: a QB change in college moves the line more because of depth and system fit; Kalshi quotes may lag the news, so timing of QB vintage matters.
Spread size x blowout management: cover probability for big favorites depends on whether the coach keeps pressing, shifting the tail of the margin distribution.
Tempo mismatch x efficiency: when a fast offense meets a slow, ball-control team, variance falls and margin shrinks; spreads with high rating gaps may overstate.
Early season: low returning production x talent prior: ratings carry large uncertainty; weight talent and portal data more than last year's results.

A backup quarterback behind a depleted offensive line loses more than the sum of the two separate effects because inexperienced passers rely on protection and play-action tied to a functioning run game; the penalty is largest when the replacement is a first-year player with fewer than 50 dropbacks.

Past a lead of about 21 points in the second half the favourite's marginal scoring rate drops sharply for conservative coaches, while aggressive coaches keep scoring; this makes the cover rate for 30+ point rungs a coach-dependent step, not a smooth function of rating gap.

In weeks 1-4 the prior dominates, so talent and returning production explain more of the margin than in-season efficiency and the posterior SD is wide; from about week 8 the weights flip and the same variables become nearly redundant.

Wind or rain compresses passing, which helps a run-heavy option team against a weak front and hurts an air-raid favourite; the weather effect on margin depends on which side is pass-reliant and on opposing run defence.

Home-field value is not constant: it grows with altitude and crowd for visitors on a short week and shrinks in rivalry games where both teams are fully motivated; opt-outs at neutral-site bowls remove it altogether.

In the D3 and FCS playoffs the higher seed hosts until the final, so the home edge is confounded with seed strength and applies only in rounds before the neutral-site final; a regular-season home edge applied to a playoff host overstates the favourite when both seed and host status carry the same information.

game_moneyline_spread.label: Game moneyline and spread
game_moneyline_spread.mechanism: Margin mean = opponent-adjusted rating difference (efficiency, talent, QB-specific) + home or neutral-site edge + rest/travel/motivation, with fat tails and key numbers. Because college connectivity is thin and injury information is sparse, the market-implied rating is the primary prior and the model searches for incremental information: QB status, availability, weather, scheme style, and blowout behavior at large spreads. Overtime is certain to produce a winner so moneyline has no tie leg.
game_moneyline_spread.target: Probability a team wins (regulation plus overtime; no ties) or covers a spread rung.

Opponent-adjusted rushing efficiency gives rushing yards per attempt.
Opponent-adjusted passing efficiency gives passing yards and TDs.

Opposing secondary adjusts passing yards and explosive passes.

Havoc rates predict negative plays, forced fumbles and turnovers.
Takeaway luck regresses; use process measures to project turnover props.
Expected scoring and TD counts.

Stat definition (e.g. whether sack yards count in rushing, FBS-only) and source determine settlement.
Discrepancies between data sources.

Injury news has no reliable official feed in college football, so timing and source matter more than the designation.
Target, carry and snap share translate team volume into player volume; share changes after injuries are the main source of line error.
Receiving yards = completions x yards per completion, and completions scale with dropbacks that depend on score state, so the mean and its spread must be conditioned on expected flow.
The yardage threshold is crossed mostly in games with high snap counts; state-dependent tempo is the mechanism linking expected margin to those counts.
Sets the dispersion of per-completion yards, and so P(325+) relative to the mean.
Links availability of specific pass-catchers to team yardage via formation, instead of treating every receiver as interchangeable.
KXNCAAFTEAMRSHATT counts team rushing attempts, and KXNCAAFTEAMYDS charges sacks and kneels to rushing; both need the script-driven run-play count.
KXNCAAFTEAMYDS settles on total offense = rushing plus receiving yards with sacks and kneels as negative rushing yards, i.e. plays x net yards per play.
Small but rule-specified deduction in KXNCAAFTEAMYDS for the leading team; ignored by gross-yardage models.
TEAMTD, TOTALTD, TEAMRSHTD and TEAMRECTD settle on touchdown counts: expected scoring trips times TD per trip with the rush/pass split is the core count model.
TOTALTD and TEAMTD ladders sit in the upper tail (8+ game TDs, 5+ rushing TDs) where a Poisson understates probability; the fitted dispersion prices each rung.
KXNCAAFDSTTD settles on at least one defensive or special-teams touchdown by either team, and TOTALTD/FIRSTTDTEAM count them too.
KXNCAAFFIRSTTDTEAM is a race between the two teams' touchdown arrival processes with a No-TD outcome, priced from first-TD hazard rates.
Splits touchdowns into rushing versus receiving for TEAMRSHTD and TEAMRECTD; a fumble-recovery TD is credited to neither.

interactions.hypothesis: Pace x pass rate: yardage thresholds depend on both plays and mix, and a fast pass-heavy team inflates yards while being penalized by opponent efficiency.
Havoc x turnover luck: takeaway counts should be projected from havoc and pressure with strong regression of realized turnovers.
Spread script x rushing: favorites in lopsided games accumulate rushing yards late, pushing team rushing yards above neutral-situation projections.

A team's dropback response to being a big underdog depends on its own pass-rate slope and tempo: an air-raid, up-tempo offence converts a deficit into many extra pass snaps, while a run-first or slow team under the same deficit still burns clock; so extra receiving yards from the trailing script appear only where pass_rate slope and pace are high.

An offence that lives on deep completions has yards per completion multiplied by the opposing safeties' explosive-allowed rate, while a short-pass offence is almost insensitive to it; the product, not the sum, determines the right tail above a high strike.

Sustained wind above about 15 mph reduces deep-ball completion and shifts calls to the run, but the cut-in only appears past the threshold and is largest for vertical offences; mild weather has no effect.

Loss of a top receiver costs more yards in a four-wide scheme (where he is on the field for 90 percent of snaps and targets concentrate) than in a heavy-set scheme where targets spread across tight ends and backs; a backup quarterback shrinks the yards per target of every remaining receiver at once.

A team's rushing-touchdown count is its touchdown total times the share credited to runs inside the ten; a designed-run quarterback raises that share, and the effect is largest for offences that reach the red zone often, so the 5+ rushing-touchdown rung depends on the product rather than on either factor.

Rushing attempts respond to the non-market expected lead with a hinge: below a two-score expected lead the count tracks tempo, above it clock-killing run calls add attempts while total snaps fall, so tempo and expected margin offset each other in heavy favourites.

Under the KXNCAAFTEAMYDS accounting a sack subtracts yards from total offense, so the cost of a sack-prone quarterback scales with dropback volume: a trailing team that passes 45 times loses far more net yards to sacks than a leading team passing 20 times, and the same quarterback pulls total yards down more in chase scripts.

game_stat_props.label: Game and team stat props
game_stat_props.mechanism: Team/game stats scale with plays and style: yardage by pass/rush split and efficiency, turnovers and sacks by havoc/pressure and ball security, TDs by scoring expectation and red-zone style. The data source and stat definitions (e.g. sack yards counted against rushing, bowl stats, FBS vs FCS) matter for settlement; heavy variance from blowouts and tempo.
game_stat_props.target: Probability that a team or game statistic (yards, turnovers, sacks, TDs, first downs, etc.) meets a threshold per official stat source.

Short fields from turnovers inflate points scored; a team's recent turnover margin beyond its fumble-recovery expectation regresses, so totals built on raw scoring carry a luck premium.
Replaces the average-of-paces approach with the structural number of scoring trials, the strongest single driver of a game total.
Splits efficiency into moving and finishing, important because totals depend on 3-versus-7 outcomes rather than yardage.
Fat-tail component of the total not captured by drive-based efficiency.
Makes the weather vintage input usable for totals by linking forecast to actual game conditions in the specific building.
KXNCAAFHIGHSCORE settles on whether any Division I regular-season game (overtime included) exceeds the strike, an extreme-value quantity over all game totals that a one-game total model cannot price.

interactions.hypothesis: Combined tempo: two fast teams compound plays and drives, but a slow opponent controls clock; model pace as an interaction rather than average.
Weather x style: wind/rain reduce points more for pass-heavy and explosive teams and affect FG range, so the total effect depends on both offenses' styles.
Blowout management x spread: large spreads lower the favorite's second-half scoring but raise underdog garbage-time points; net effect depends on coach behavior.
Success vs explosiveness x havoc: an explosive offense facing a high-havoc defense has more failed drives but more big plays, widening the total distribution.

Possession count depends on run share through the clock rules: a run-heavy team that keeps the clock moving after first downs shortens the game for both sides, and a pass-heavy opponent cannot restore the possessions because incompletions stop the clock only for its own snaps; so tempo of the faster team matters less when the slower team has a high run share.

Wind above roughly 15 mph at an open stadium reduces both deep passing and field-goal range beyond 40 yards; the cut in total is minimal below the threshold and then steep, and is amplified when the kicker is already marginal.

In a one-sided game the total follows a different regime: the leader's scoring drops but the trailing team's garbage-time possessions and return touchdowns add points; whether the total goes up or down depends on the coach's pull point and on trailing-team passing.

A high-explosiveness offence facing a high-havoc defence produces many failed drives but occasional long scores; the mean total changes little while its variance and right tail increase, which matters for high rungs.

A quarterback change lowers both efficiency and tempo (backups run a simpler script), so the effect on the total is the product of a smaller points-per-drive and fewer possessions, and it is bigger for up-tempo offences.

game_total.label: Game total points
game_total.mechanism: Total = possessions x points per possession for both teams. In college, tempo spans a wider range, clock rules and style (option, air raid) change plays per game, and mismatch/blowout management lowers the favorite's late scoring while inflating variance; weather and QB identity are the main late-information drivers. Distribution has key numbers and fat right tail; the Kalshi ladder should be consistent with the implied distribution.
game_total.target: Probability that total points exceed a rung (regulation plus overtime per wording).

The existing coaching input measures tenure and scheme but not the one decision that converts a close game into overtime.
Sets the conditional probability of a second and later overtime period, which compounds geometrically into the 9+ period contract.
Only the rule regime of OT 3+ makes 9+ periods possible, and its per-period tie probability depends on exactly this quantity.
Turns a per-game tail probability into the season contract and handles the monotone state variable (record already set).

interactions.hypothesis: Spread near zero x low total: overtime probability peaks for evenly matched, low-scoring games and is nearly flat for large spreads.
Coach end-of-game decisions x kicker: teams that settle for a tie-breaking or tying FG vs go for win change overtime odds in the final minutes.
Pace x variance: fewer possessions increase the share of games within a score at the end, boosting tie probability.

Tie probability depends jointly on the absolute rating gap and the margin SD, which in turn depends on possessions and weather; at a gap of zero the probability rises as SD falls, but at a gap of seven it rises with SD, so the sign of the SD effect flips with the gap.

A coach who habitually kicks the tying field goal creates overtime only if his kicker is accurate from 35-45 yards; a poor kicker makes the decision pointless, so incidence of created ties depends on the product of intent and capability.

The probability that a period ends tied switches regime at the third overtime from a score-matching process (0.25-0.35) to a two-point match (about 0.5), so survival to 9 periods multiplies a small early factor by a roughly 0.5^6 tail; both the regime and the number of games enter the season probability.

Overtime ties are more likely when both offences are poor from the 25 or both kickers are reliable (both score a field goal), and wind lowers touchdown probability while leaving short field goals reachable; the period tie probability is a product-sum of both teams' scoring distributions.

overtime.label: Overtime occurrence and overtime length
overtime.mechanism: Overtime occurs when regulation ends tied: probability = mass of the final-margin distribution at exactly zero, which is concentrated in close spreads and kicker-driven scoring, and sensitive to the lattice of college scoring (3, 6, 7, 8) and late-game decisions (kneel, go-for-it, field goal at end). Rule mechanics (25-yard start, alternating possessions, 2-point attempts from later periods) determine length and extra-period markets. Market wording must define overtime as an extra period played.
overtime.target: Probability that the game goes to overtime (and potentially to multiple overtimes) as defined in the contract.

inputs.why: Full-game strength prior is the starting point for period margin means.

Adjusted defense determines early and late-period suppression.
Team-specific first versus second-half profile determines period margins relative to game margin.

Receiving first shifts the first quarter and the order of second-half possessions.
Scripted opening-drive efficiency gives early-period edge.
Second-half behavior of a leading team determines whether the half margin shrinks.
QB identity shifts early scripted efficiency and period margins.
Depth at tails matters in second halves.
Halftime adjustments and tempo.
Period margin residual distribution (with tie mass) is required for spread and ML at periods.
Treatment of ties for period winners (push or loss) and overtime exclusion define settlement.
Quarter and half legs share the game script so period margins are correlated with the game margin; model jointly.
One early turnover decides a quarter; regressing turnover luck separates repeatable offence from noise in 15-minute sample.
Possession count in a quarter is the dominant source of difference between a quarter spread and a share of the game spread.
Q2 and Q4 spreads and highest-scoring-quarter markets depend on these abnormal drives, which are not in a season efficiency rating.

The same rules text contrast (2H includes OT, 4Q excludes it) changes the target distribution by series; a series-specific spillover makes the difference explicit.

interactions.hypothesis: Talent depth x period: more talented teams win second halves via depth and rotation, so depth matters more in H2 than in Q1.
Opening possession x first-half margin: receiving first adds expected margin to first quarter and shifts half-end possession order.
Blowout behavior x second-half spread: favorites' second-half margins shrink when leading big, requiring conditional distribution on halftime lead.

Expected points in a period equal possessions times scoring rate, so receiving the opening kickoff matters much more for an offence with a high touchdown rate: the extra drive is worth about 0.5 times that team's points per drive, a bigger edge for an elite offence than for a poor one.

Hypothesis, not a demonstrated effect: second-half margins depend on halftime state: when the leader is up three scores, depth and rotation determine whether the margin shrinks, grows or stays; below that lead the first-half dynamics persist, so the regime switches at roughly 21 points. The input cfb.blowout_management is itself audited WEAK, so this regime switch is a conjecture to test, not a basis for the model.

End-of-half scoring depends on possession order and whether a team plays to score or holds the ball: the team receiving the second-half kickoff has an incentive to hold for a field goal before the half, raising the other team's chance of scoring in Q2.

Hypothesis, not a demonstrated effect: a backup quarterback is scripted conservatively in Q1, so Q1 margin shrinks toward zero, but only if the offence's opening script was prepared for him; once the game opens up in later quarters the penalty grows, so the effect of a QB change on period margin depends on the period index.

The 2H winner and the full-game winner are strongly dependent through overtime, and 2H sides depend on the 1H result through halftime-lead script; marginal quarters are positively correlated through team strength but only weakly so, which defeats independent-leg pricing.

The KXNCAAF1HWINNER Tie strike and the two team strikes partition the half-time margin, so their probabilities must sum to one; the tie mass at the half is raised by end-of-half field-goal drives that equalise 7-10 or 14-17 scores and lowered when the team holding the last first-half possession is an efficient two-minute offence, so the three legs move jointly with the end-of-half possession order.

quarter_and_half_sides.label: Quarter and half moneyline and spread
quarter_and_half_sides.mechanism: Period margin mean is a fraction of the game margin (not proportional): favorites win first halves more reliably because starters and scripted plays dominate early, while second-half margins depend on blowout management, adjustments and depth. Period margin has high variance relative to mean, a large tie mass for quarters, and depends on opening possession and QB/personnel. Settlement of ties (push, no-action or lose) is critical.
quarter_and_half_sides.target: Probability a team leads/wins or covers a spread in a specific half or quarter (period margin, ties per wording).

interactions.hypothesis: Opening possession x first-drive scripts: Q1 totals depend on both who receives and how scripted drives perform.
Lead size x second-half pace: second-half totals fall when a favorite leads by 3 scores; scale by coach behavior.
End-of-half scoring x tempo: fast teams get extra possessions at end of the first half, lifting Q2 totals.

Probability of crossing the 7.5 rung in a quarter jumps when the combined drive count falls from six to four, because with four drives it takes two scoring drives for more than seven points and the zero-scoring mass rises sharply; the effect of tempo is non-linear and strongest for slow-tempo pairings.

Fourth-quarter share of the game total depends on the expected gap: when the gap is small, Q4 holds the highest share (two-minute drills, urgency); when large, the leader's rate falls and the trailer's garbage-time scores partially offset, so Q4 share turns down.

End-of-half field-goal decisions interact with kicker range: a coach with a reliable kicker takes three points before the half, which raises Q2 and Q4 totals in lumps of three and thickens the pmf at 3 and 10, while an unreliable kicker leads to turnovers on downs and thinner mass at 3.

Wind that rises in the second half cuts the passing offence's scoring rate and the effect is amplified for fast-tempo pass-heavy offences, so the second-half total responds to the product of forecast wind trend and offensive pass reliance, not to the average forecast.

The overtime increment exists only in games tied after regulation, which are close games where starters stay in and the 2H regulation total is least compressed by blowout management; so the increment is not independent of the regulation second-half total and adds right-tail mass exactly where the 6.5 rung is least at risk.

Q2 and Q4 gain end-of-half drives and tempo spikes, so in high-total games they are the likeliest argmax, while in low-total games a single touchdown decides the highest quarter and ties among 7-point quarters are common; the drive budget per quarter therefore changes both the argmax probability and the expected tie split.

quarter_and_half_totals.label: Quarter and half totals and team totals
quarter_and_half_totals.mechanism: Period totals = period possessions x points per possession, allocated from the game total by period shares: first-quarter scripted drives and opening possession, end-of-half scoring, second-half tempo and substitution patterns (blowouts), and halftime adjustments. College second-half totals depend heavily on lead size and coach behavior. Short periods have lumpy scoring (0, 3, 7), so exact distribution matters.
quarter_and_half_totals.target: Probability that points in a quarter/half (game or one team) exceed a rung.

interactions.hypothesis: Committee preferences x results: berth probability depends on the quality of wins and strength-of-record language; losses late weigh more than early.
Schedule x conference tiebreakers: remaining head-to-head games determine tiebreakers non-linearly.
QB injury risk x top-heavy contenders: title odds concentrate in teams with a single dominant QB, so injury scenarios dominate variance.

Playoff berth probability is a steep step in the number of losses: a team with zero or one loss is very likely in, a team with three losses rarely, and which side of the step the team lands on depends on who the losses came against and when; the committee's treatment of one loss also depends on conference championship status.

A contender's title odds are a mixture over quarterback health states: with the starter its rating is high, with the backup it falls several points, and the draws shared across games produce fat tails; top-heavy contenders (one dominant quarterback) have more mass in the downside branch.

Conference championship qualification depends on unbalanced schedules and head-to-head tiebreakers: a team that has already beaten its closest rival holds the tiebreaker and needs fewer wins, so remaining head-to-head games have asymmetric value that a simple expected-wins model misses.

Over a four-year horizon the contribution of current talent decays toward a program mean while portal and revenue resources renew it; the incremental value of an extra recruiting-class point is large in year one and small by year four.

Selection rules differ between seasons (field size, automatic bids for champions, seed construction) so the same resume gives different berth probability under different formats; contracts for the same season must use the format regime in force, and the 24-team expansion market implies a possible future regime.

For KXNCAAFLSUTEX2X the regular-season result changes the second leg: an LSU win lifts LSU's CFP odds and lowers Texas's, and the two must then land in opposite bracket halves; the probability of the rematch final conditional on the first result is far from the unconditional rematch probability, so the product of marginals misprices it.

A strong offence's expected total keeps rising with rating gap only until a three-score lead; beyond that, conservative coaches cut the team's points while persistent coaches keep scoring, so the response to rating gap flattens at a coach-specific level.

interactions.hypothesis: Team TD pool x role share: share depends on the expected game script; trailing teams pass more near goal line, shifting TD probability from RBs to WRs.
QB mobility x goal-line carries: mobile QBs absorb TDs, lowering RB scoring odds even with high red-zone volume.
Blowout x depth: in lopsided games backups score late, raising anytime TD for backups and lowering for starters pulled early.

Team rushing touchdowns equal TD count times rushing share, and the rushing share is higher with a mobile quarterback and a power-run goal-line mix; both the count and the share vary across teams, so the product has more spread than either factor.

In a one-sided game the leading team runs near the goal line and uses backups, raising the rushing share and total TD count for the leader, while the trailing team throws and adds receiving touchdowns; the combined effect on high-count tails depends on the gap.

First-TD probability depends on the receiving team's head start and each team's early hazard, and defensive touchdowns add a third arrival channel that can reverse the order when the opposing offence is turnover-prone; the three are not independent because the same offence both scores and turns over.

A defensive or special-teams touchdown flips the game script, and the knock-on effect on the opponent's passing and rushing touchdown counts depends on the pre-game expected margin: it is large in an evenly matched game where the scorer's lead changes the trailing team's play mix, and small when the scorer is already a heavy favourite or the opponent is far behind anyway.

cfb.bowl_selection_state.label: Bowl eligibility, slot balance and conference tie-in selection model
cfb.bowl_selection_state.measurement: For each draw of cfb.rating_posterior_draws simulate remaining games. Per team: countable_wins = wins over FBS opponents + min(1, wins over FCS opponents that averaged >= 90% of the permissible maximum football grants-in-aid per year over the rolling two-year period, i.e. >= 56.7, or hold an approved waiver); wins over non-Division I opponents, ties and forfeits = 0. Deserving if countable_wins >= overall regular-season losses (12 games: 6-6; 13 games: 7-6, a 6-7 team is an alternate); a loss in the conference championship game does not remove deserving status. Reclassifying FCS-to-FBS programs are treated as regular FBS members from 2026 (Proposal 2026-31). Remove the CFP field first, then allocate deserving teams in each season's bowl pick order: each bowl takes the best remaining team of its tie-in conference by score = countable_wins + 0.5 x (AP-ranked flag) + logit draw term (multinomial logit on wins, rank, conference, travel distance fitted on 2014-2025 selections). If deserving teams < open slots, fill in the legislated order: (1) teams whose only shortfall is a non-qualifying FCS win with a denied waiver, (2) 13-game 6-7 teams, (3) 5-7 teams with a multiyear APR permitting postseason play; for 2026 onward the unfilled tie-in's conference picks its own 5-7 team by the same score (no APR order), for 2014-2025 backtests use descending multiyear APR. Output P(selected) per team and P(deserving < slots) per season. Re-run weekly as of latest results; no market input.
cfb.bowl_selection_state.mechanism: KXNCAAFBOWLGAME settles on being selected (not playing) for a certified bowl or the CFP. Chain: countable wins (wins over FBS opponents plus at most one win over an FCS opponent averaging 90% of the maximum football grants-in-aid over two years, Bylaw 18.7.2.1.1) -> deserving status (countable wins >= overall losses, e.g. 6-6; a deserving team that loses its conference title game stays deserving) -> CFP field removed -> conference tie-in allocation -> if deserving teams < open slots, legislated alternates (denied-waiver FCS-win teams, 13-game 6-7 teams, then 5-7 teams with a postseason-eligible multiyear APR, no longer in APR order after Proposal 2026-30).
cfb.bowl_selection_state.rationale: Selection is not a function of raw wins: a second FCS win, or a win over an FCS team that did not average 90 percent of the permissible maximum grants-in-aid over a rolling two-year period (56.7 per year under the post-House-settlement Q&A; waiver possible for catastrophic cases), does not count, so a 6-6 team can be ineligible. Tie or forfeited games do not count. When slots exceed deserving teams, alternates follow a legislated order; Proposal 2026-30 (FBSOC May 2026, DI Cabinet June 23-24 2026 'Adopted (Final)') removed the descending-APR ordering of 5-7 alternates, so the conference with the unfilled tie-in chooses among its APR-eligible 5-7 teams, and Proposal 2026-31 made programs reclassifying from FCS to FBS bowl-eligible. A 6-6 mid-major is a bubble case while a 7-5 power team is safe.

cfb.period_margin_lattice.mechanism: Empirical probabilities of period margin = 0, positive margins up to 8+, by period and by pre-game expected margin and total.

cfb.period_possession_allocation.label: Period possession allocation (opening kick, deferral and end-of-half order)
cfb.period_possession_allocation.measurement: Per head coach: P(defer | wins toss) over last 3 seasons, shrunk with k = 10 tosses to the conference mean (remaining mass = receive; ignore choosing the end). P(win toss) = 0.5. P(team A receives first) = 0.5 x (1 - defer_A) + 0.5 x defer_B, and P(team A receives second half) = 1 - that. Expected drives in quarter k per team = season mean drives per team x quarter share (0.24-0.26) with Q1 and Q3 adjusted by +0.5 drive for the receiving-first team (Q1) or second-half receiver (Q3). Record realised toss only after kickoff; before that use the probabilities.
cfb.period_possession_allocation.mechanism: Expected possessions per team in each quarter given who receives the opening kickoff, deferral habits and tempo.
cfb.period_possession_allocation.rationale: A quarter has only about 2-3 possessions per team, and receiving the opening kickoff gives one extra drive in Q1 (and typically ends Q2 with the other team holding the ball); the share swings expected quarter margin by 0.3 to 0.8 points between the two possession orders. The toss itself is only known at kickoff, so the input must be probabilistic.

interactions.hypothesis: Team rank multiplies a candidate's production in voter perception.
Efficiency against weak schedules is discounted by voters.
Quarterback status changes the candidate's late-season production.

An award candidate's chance is the product of leading the visible production race and staying healthy: a candidate with a small production lead and high workload faces a higher chance of falling behind because of injury, so the joint of current gap, workload and hazard shapes the probability more than the gap alone.

Voters weight statistics by team success and discount production against weak schedules, so a candidate's effective support is production percentile times a team-rank factor times a schedule discount; the same stats on a ranked team and an unranked team yield very different vote shares.

Hypothesis to test: a coach who beats expectation by many wins wins only if the team also finishes ranked or wins a title; above a threshold of wins above expectation the probability jumps, and below it conference rank decides.

For the AP conference Defensive Player of the Year, voters reward sack and tackle-for-loss leaders much more when the player's team is ranked or contending; a high pass-rush production rate on a losing team converts to fewer votes, so the production effect is conditional on team record.

Remaining schedule changes a candidate's projected production before the ballot, and for a receiver it also depends on whether his starting quarterback keeps playing; a Biletnikoff candidate with an easy remaining schedule gains only if his team keeps passing at the same rate.

interactions.hypothesis: Exit probability rises when record falls short of preseason expectation, especially late in the season.
Portal-window timing concentrates transfer announcements.
Rivalry losses raise exit risk beyond record alone.

A poor season raises the firing hazard but a large buyout multiplies it down, so the hazard is the product of performance shortfall and affordability; a coach with a 10 win shortfall and a 40 million dollar buyout is about as likely to survive as one with a smaller shortfall and no buyout.

The hazard changes regime at the end of the regular season: before rivalry week exits are rare, after the final regular-season game and after bowls they cluster, so the cumulative probability to Dec 1 is dominated by the last two weeks while to Feb 1 it includes the post-bowl wave.

CFP approval jumps when declared support crosses the voting threshold and the calendar allows a meeting; until then the probability is low regardless of rhetoric, so the key variable is votes relative to the threshold, not general support.

A candidate's hire probability depends on his own school's buyout and whether his current team is still playing, since coaches in the playoff or bowl cannot be hired until the season ends; the timing hazard and the candidate identity are interdependent.

A conference move has zero probability before the grant-of-rights, notice and membership-vote constraints allow it and a small positive hazard afterwards, so the response to reported talks is piecewise in the date and in the constraint state; the same rumor means very different things before and after the feasibility date.

For a player listed in both KXNCAAFTRANSFER and a draft-declaration market, the declare leg of the transfer market and the DRAFTDECLARE YES are one event, so the transfer destination probabilities must be conditional on not declaring and the two markets must sum consistently.

interactions.hypothesis: A half lead protects less when the leader is the weaker team: reversal probability rises with the pre-game gap against the half leader.
Wind or rain lowers half scoring and raises the zero-margin mass, enlarging every Tie 1H cell non-linearly.
Starter removal after a large half lead truncates second-half margin and pushes reversal cells toward zero beyond what rate models imply.

The team that usually receives the second-half kickoff (the one that did not take the opening kick) gets the first second-half possession after a tied half, tilting the two tie-at-half cells toward it beyond the rating gap.

The probability that the half leader holds on depends on who leads: a 7-point half lead by a 17-point favourite converts at very high rates, the same lead by an underdog converts far less often because the stronger team gets more second-half scoring drives. The reversal cell is a function of half margin and gap jointly, not additive.

Sustained wind above about 15 mph and heavy rain lower first-half scoring; the probability of a tied half rises faster than linearly as expected half total falls toward 14 because 0-0, 3-3 and 7-7 halves become common.

Once the half lead exceeds about three scores, backups enter during the third quarter and the leader stops scoring, but the trailing team also faces a large deficit; reversal cells collapse to near zero above that threshold while margin cells become unreliable.

After a tied half, the team receiving the second-half kickoff gets the first and often an extra possession; its conditional win probability is higher than the opponent's at equal strength, so the two tie-at-half cells split unevenly by who deferred.

A trailing team that both speeds up and goes for it on fourth down raises second-half variance on two axes; the comeback probability scales with the product of extra drives and per-drive upside, so an aggressive up-tempo underdog fattens reversal cells far more than either trait alone.

half_full_double_result.label: CFB half-time/full-time double result
half_full_double_result.mechanism: Each market is one cell of a six-cell partition (3 half states x 2 full-game winners): first-half result (team A leads, tie, team B leads) crossed with the full-game winner, which always exists because overtime is included. The cell probability is P(half state) times P(full winner | half state). The first factor comes from a lumpy half-margin distribution built from the strength gap, team half-scoring splits and possession order; the second comes from second-half and overtime play given the half state, where leaders slow down, trailing teams take risk, starters are pulled in blowouts, and the team that did not receive the opening kickoff usually receives the second-half kickoff (toss winners normally defer, so this is a convention, not a rule). Reversal cells (half leader loses) and tie-at-half cells carry the mass a product of marginals misprices.
half_full_double_result.target: Probability of a stated (1st-half result, full-game result) pair, half ties allowed, full game incl. OT.

interactions.hypothesis: An error in one conference offset moves legs in opposite directions when the backed sides sit on opposite sides of it (Big Ten beating SEC versus Big 12 beating Big Ten), and in the same direction when they sit on the same side; pair dependence takes either sign.
Underdog-cover-and-under dependence is strongest when the expected margin sits near the spread strike and weak for large mismatches.
Opt-outs add leg-specific strength loss with wide uncertainty; in postseason packs this inflates posterior spread per leg and the joint tail.

In the sampled 3- and 4-leg packs the legs load on different conferences: Indiana over Alabama backs Big Ten against SEC, Texas Tech over Oregon backs Big 12 against Big Ten, Georgia over Ole Miss is intra-SEC, and in the 4-leg pack Ohio St. over Miami (FL) backs Big Ten against ACC, on the same side as Indiana. An offset error therefore pushes opposed legs in opposite directions (negative dependence: the all-hit probability is below the product of the leg probabilities whatever the sign of the realised error) and same-side legs together; the sign follows the signed exposure.

With few expected possessions, scoring variance shrinks for both margin and total, so an underdog +7.5 and under 48.5 become strongly positively dependent; with many possessions the margin variance grows while the under is unlikely, and the dependence weakens.

For favourite-cover-plus-over combinations, the joint grows with the strength gap until the favourite's lead triggers starter removal; beyond that point the total stalls while margin is capped, so the joint flattens.

Losing a starting QB or several draft-bound starters reduces leg win probability proportionally; because the pack multiplies legs, the pack price falls by the same factor, and simultaneous news on two legs compounds.

Long postseason layoffs (three to five weeks) add uncertainty to team strength that is absent in the regular season, so posterior spread per leg widens and the pack's distribution moves toward the extremes in postseason regimes.

multi_leg_parlay_packs.label: College football pre-packaged parlays (multi-game moneyline and same-game combos)
multi_leg_parlay_packs.mechanism: A pack pays only if every leg hits, so its probability is the joint of leg events, not a single game outcome. For multi-game moneyline packs each leg is a game winner (always decided via overtime); legs are independent in game noise but share rating-model error through conference offsets in cross-conference postseason games; the dependence is signed by the conference exposure of each backed side (a Big Ten offset error helps a leg backing Indiana over Alabama and hurts a leg backing Texas Tech over Oregon), and opt-out waves add slate-wide shocks. Inputs apply by contract type: cross-game inputs (cross_game_residual_dependence, rating_posterior_draws, cross_conf_calibration, rest_travel) to the 2/3/4-leg moneyline packs; margin_total_joint_pmf, expected_possessions, weather_pit, blowout_management to the same-game pack. For same-game packs the legs (spread cover and total side) are strongly dependent through pace and score state: underdog cover pairs with the under, favourite cover with the over. Errors in each leg compound multiplicatively, so calibration of every leg and of the dependence matters more than in a single-game market.
multi_leg_parlay_packs.target: Probability that every leg of a pre-packaged combination resolves YES jointly: several named teams all win their games, or a spread cover and a total side in the same game both hit.

One missed game costs a player about one game of expected production. If the leader's cushion exceeds that, a single absence rarely flips the race; if it is below, a missed game hands the lead over. The effect of injury risk on price therefore jumps around a gap of one game's production.

Better teams run more plays and score more, raising a feature back's volume, but in blowouts the starter sits for the fourth quarter. Expected season carries rise with team strength and then flatten or fall for heavy favourites, favouring leaders on good-not-dominant teams.

season_stat_leader.label: CFB season stat leader
season_stat_leader.mechanism: A leader market is an order statistic: each eligible player's end-of-regular-season total equals the current total plus remaining production, and YES requires the named player's total to be the maximum. Remaining production is games remaining (byes, Hawaii exemption, cancellations; conference title games excluded) times participation times volume share of team plays times efficiency against remaining opponents, with overdispersed game-to-game variation. Teammates compete for the same carries or targets; QB health links receivers to passers; sacks depend on opponents' dropbacks. Late in the season the current gap dominates; early, usage and health do. Ties pay $1/N, which matters for small-integer stats. The season_outcome blueprint inputs (standings, playoff format, polls, futures coherence, market ratings) were not carried over: they describe team outcomes, and the inputs here are player-volume inputs for an order statistic.
season_stat_leader.target: Probability that a named player finishes the regular season as the leader of a stated counting stat (rushing yards, receiving yards, passing touchdowns, sacks) in a conference or in Division I, with ties paying $1/N.

Expected sacks equal dropbacks times pressure rate times sack-given-pressure, and a mobile quick-release quarterback cuts the third factor, so the pass rush's advantage is large only against a quarterback who holds the ball; the effect is multiplicative in the volume.

A field goal beyond about 40 yards is sharply less likely in a headwind of 15 mph or more, so wind turns long attempts into punts or fourth-down tries and both lowers makes and shifts attempts, which a make-rate adjustment alone misses.

Two-point attempts occur after touchdowns and are concentrated in specific score-differential states (down 8, up 17, trailing late), so the count depends on touchdowns and on the state at the time; a team that scores often when trailing is likely to try more.

Delays cluster in afternoon and evening games in warm months at open stadiums; the hazard is near zero in domes and cold weather, and the regime depends on the season month and stadium type, so a single weather forecast variable is not enough.

team_event_counting_specials.label: College football team and event counting specials
team_event_counting_specials.mechanism: Team counts are plays times a rate: turnovers and sacks follow opponent dropbacks and the pass-rush versus protection matchup, field goals follow stalled drives inside the kicker's range, two-point tries follow score and coaching tendency.
